privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.q1: What private information about me do you collect?
privacy.a1: None. Besides IP address and browser which is stored in logs for every internet service, we do not collect any form of private information such as your name, email or address.
privacy.q2: What do you store in cookies?
privacy.a2: Nothing. We do not use cookies. We use persistent local storage called IndexedDB for the storage of your wallet.
privacy.q3: How do you collect analytics information?
privacy.a3: We do not. We do not use any form of analytics service, e.g. google analytics, so that you can feel safer. The website is purely HTML with javascript. We do know your IP address only when you make requests to the server. Depending on your settings and your algod server or indexer, the selected server also may know your IP address.
privacy.q4: Does use of this service affect the ads I see?
privacy.a4: No. Ad servers do not have any information from us about any usage. The only way how, e.g. google, may know you are using this service is if you access this site from google search.

faq.subtitle: Everything you need to know about {name}, Algorand and the Biatec ecosystem - from your first account to swaps, security and DApp connections.

general.title: General Questions
general.q1: What is {name} and what is it for?
general.a1: {name} is a free, open-source, non-custodial wallet for the Algorand blockchain (and Algorand-based networks such as Voi) that runs entirely in your web browser. It lets you create and manage accounts, send and receive ALGO and other assets, swap tokens, and sign transactions for decentralized applications - without ever handing your private keys to a third party. "Non-custodial" means only you control the keys, so only you can move the funds.
general.q2: Do I need to register or provide personal information to use {name}?
general.a2: No. {name} has no backend server, no sign-up form and no KYC. Accounts are generated and stored locally in your browser, so you can start immediately without giving up your email, phone number or identity documents. The flip side is that nobody can reset your password or recover your account for you - see the Backup section below.
general.a3: Yes, {name} is completely free and open source. You only pay the small network fee that every blockchain transaction requires (on Algorand the minimum is 0.001 ALGO), and that fee goes to the network, not to the wallet.
general.q4: Which devices and browsers does {name} work on?
general.a4: {name} is a responsive web application that works in any modern desktop or mobile browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) without installation. Because it is a single-page app with no native binary, the same wallet works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS. Your wallet is stored per browser, so use a backup file to move it to another browser or device.
general.a5: {name} was originally created by Scholtz & Company, jsa. and is now developed under the {link1} brand. The project is open source, and anyone can review, audit or contribute to the code on {link2}.
general.a6: Algorand Mainnet is the default. You can also switch to Voi Mainnet, Aramid Mainnet, Algorand Testnet and, for developers, local Devnet or Sandbox networks from the network selector in the Settings. Testnet coins have no monetary value and are meant for experimenting risk-free. Always check which network is selected before you send anything.

biatec.title: Biatec Wallet & Ecosystem
biatec.a1: {link1} is the company and brand behind {name}, building a suite of open tools around the Algorand blockchain, including this wallet, a swap/exchange routing service and a scheduled-payments service, all designed to make using Algorand simpler and safer.
biatec.q2: How does Biatec Wallet relate to Biatec's other services?
biatec.a2: Biatec Wallet is the entry point: it holds your keys and signs transactions locally, while other {link1} (such as the swap router used on the Swap page, or the scheduled-payments API used for recurring transfers) only ever receive unsigned transaction data or public information - never your private keys.
biatec.q3: Does Biatec run its own Algorand infrastructure?
biatec.a3: Yes. {link1} operates its own Algorand node, indexer and participation infrastructure that {name} can connect to, in addition to public Algorand nodes, giving you a choice of network providers directly in the wallet's settings.
biatec.q4: What is the Biatec swap router used for?
biatec.a4: When you use the Swap feature in {name}, your request is routed through {link1} aggregator, which compares prices across multiple Algorand decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to find you the best available rate, then returns an unsigned transaction for you to review and sign yourself.
biatec.q5: Is Biatec funded by Algorand Inc. or the Algorand Foundation?
biatec.a5: Biatec is an independent, community-driven project - it is not owned by, and does not receive ongoing funding from, Algorand Inc. or the Algorand Foundation. It has, however, received several one-off grants through the Algorand Foundation's {link1}, including grants for {name} itself, for {link2}, and for Biatec DEX. The Algorand name and logo are used under Algorand's official media guidelines, purely to indicate blockchain compatibility.

blockchain.title: Algorand & Blockchain Basics
blockchain.a1: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-resistant public ledger maintained by many independent computers (nodes) instead of a single company or bank. Transactions are grouped into blocks, each cryptographically linked to the previous one and copied across the network, so nobody can quietly rewrite history.
blockchain.q2: What is Algorand and why does {name} use it?
blockchain.a2: Algorand is a fast, low-fee public blockchain that uses a Pure Proof-of-Stake consensus, so there is no energy-hungry mining. A new block is produced roughly every 3 seconds and, once confirmed, is final - the chain does not fork and confirmed transactions are not rolled back. It also has built-in support for tokens (ASAs) and smart contracts (run by the Algorand Virtual Machine, AVM).
blockchain.q3: What is a public/private key pair?
blockchain.a3: Every Algorand account is a pair of cryptographic keys: a public key (which becomes your address and is safe to share) and a private key (your secret, which must never be shared). The private key proves ownership by signing transactions. Anyone who has it can spend your funds, so protecting it is the most important part of using a wallet.
blockchain.q4: What is a wallet, and does it "store" my coins?
blockchain.a4: A wallet does not actually hold your coins - your ALGO and assets always live on the blockchain itself. A wallet like {name} stores and protects your private keys, shows your balances and signs the transactions that move funds recorded on-chain.
blockchain.q5: What are transaction fees on Algorand, and why are they so low?
blockchain.a5: Algorand has a very small minimum fee of 0.001 ALGO (a fraction of a cent) per transaction, and in normal conditions that is all you pay - it does not spike with the price of ALGO or with popularity like auction-based fees on other chains. Some transactions that use more network resources, such as larger post-quantum signatures, can require a higher fee, and the wallet shows you the exact fee before you sign.
blockchain.q6: Can a blockchain transaction be reversed or cancelled?
blockchain.a6: No. Once a transaction is confirmed (about 3 seconds on Algorand) it is final. There is no bank, support desk or chargeback process that can undo it. That is why you should always double-check the receiver address, the amount, the asset and the network before signing, and send a small test amount first when moving large sums to a new address.
blockchain.q7: What is ALGO and what do I need it for?
blockchain.a7: ALGO is Algorand's native coin. You need a small amount of it in every account to pay transaction fees and to satisfy the account's minimum balance (see the Assets section). ALGO is also used in Algorand governance and by node runners who secure the network. Other tokens on Algorand (such as stablecoins) are separate assets and cannot pay the fee on their own.
blockchain.q8: What is a block explorer and when should I use one?
blockchain.a8: A block explorer is a public website that lets you look up any address, transaction, asset or smart contract on the blockchain. Use it to confirm that a payment arrived, to inspect who created an asset, or to double-check what a DApp asked you to sign. Everything on a public blockchain is visible, so your addresses and balances are public even though your identity is not attached to them.

ecosystem.title: Algorand & Voi Ecosystem
ecosystem.q1: What is Voi and how is it related to Algorand?
ecosystem.a1: Voi is a separate community-owned Layer 1 blockchain built on Algorand's technology and the same virtual machine (AVM). It has its own network, its own coin (VOI), its own validators and its own tokens and apps. Because it uses the same technology, accounts, addresses and most wallet features work in a very similar way, and you can switch to Voi Mainnet in the network settings of {name}.
ecosystem.q2: Can I use the same account on Algorand and on Voi?
ecosystem.a2: Yes, the same private key produces the same address on both networks. But the networks are completely separate ledgers: ALGO on Algorand and VOI on Voi are different coins with separate balances, and sending funds on one network never moves them to the other. Always check the selected network before you send, and do not send a token to an address on a network that the receiver is not using.
ecosystem.a3: ARCs (Algorand Requests for Comments) are community standards that describe how wallets, apps and tools should behave on Algorand so they work together - for example how NFT metadata is structured (ARC-3), how smart-contract methods are described (ARC-4), how HD wallets derive accounts (ARC-52) or how a DApp asks a wallet to sign data (ARC-60). Voi follows the same standards.
ecosystem.q4: What is the ARC-56 registry and why does {name} use it?
ecosystem.a4: When a DApp asks you to sign a smart-contract call, the transaction itself only contains raw bytes - the method name and arguments are not readable. An ARC-56 file is a public description of a contract's methods and arguments. The {link1} collects such files from public GitHub repositories and links each one to the exact compiled contract program it produces. {name} looks up the contract you are about to call and, when there is a match, shows the real method name, readable arguments and which GitHub projects published the source code.
ecosystem.q5: What does the risk icon next to "Sign all" mean?
ecosystem.a5: It is a quick summary of the ARC-56 registry check for the smart-contract calls in the request. Trusted means the contract's program is registered and its publisher looks reputable; caution means something could not be verified (for example the contract is unregistered, unknown, the registry could not be reached, or a publisher is on the ban list); not verifiable means the calls do not follow the standard ABI format. Hover over the icon for the reasons. It only covers the app calls - always review the other transactions yourself.
ecosystem.q6: Does a "verified" registry result mean a contract is safe?
ecosystem.a6: No. It only means the contract you are calling matches source code that someone published on GitHub, so you can see what it claims to do and who wrote it. It is not a security audit, and a registered contract can still contain bugs or be malicious. Treat it as one useful signal, together with the DApp's reputation, audits and your own understanding of the transaction.
ecosystem.q7: What is an ARC-200 token, and how is it different from an ASA?
ecosystem.a7: An ASA is a token built into the Algorand protocol itself. An ARC-200 token is a token implemented by a smart contract, similar to ERC-20 tokens on Ethereum. ARC-200 tokens are common on Voi and can have custom logic, but they are only as trustworthy as the contract behind them. {name} can show ARC-200 balances and send them.
ecosystem.q8: What is Algorand governance and xGov?
ecosystem.a8: Algorand governance lets ALGO holders vote on the direction of the ecosystem, and xGov is a program in which community members review and vote on funding proposals for projects that build on Algorand. To take part in governance, you commit ALGO from your account for a period; the funds stay in your control and are not sent to anyone. {name} contains tools to help you take part.

security.title: Security & Privacy
security.q1: How is my wallet data secured?
security.a1: Your data never leaves your browser. Every wallet is encrypted with AES-256 using a key derived from your password (with PBKDF2) before it is saved into your browser's local IndexedDB storage. With a strong, unique password, brute-forcing the encryption is computationally infeasible. A weak or reused password is the weakest link, so choose a long, random one.
security.q2: Does my wallet password ever get sent over the internet?
security.a2: Never. Your password is used only locally to encrypt and decrypt your wallet in the browser and is never transmitted to any server, including Biatec's own infrastructure.
security.q3: What happens if I close the browser tab or my computer sleeps?
security.a3: {name} automatically locks itself and clears the decrypted data from memory after 5 minutes without activity, so a device left unattended does not leave your wallet exposed. You need to enter your password again to unlock it.
security.q4: What should I do if I suspect my device is compromised?
security.a4: From a clean, trusted device, immediately move your funds to a new account whose recovery phrase has never touched the compromised device. A private key that may have been exposed can never be made secure again - only replaced. Also revoke any WalletConnect sessions you do not recognize, and change the passwords you used on that device.
security.a5: Security audit reports are published openly in the project's GitHub repository, so anyone can review what was checked and what was found. Audits reduce risk but never remove it, which is why the code is open source for everyone to inspect.
security.q6: Who should I share my recovery phrase (mnemonic) with?
security.a6: Nobody, ever. Anyone who knows your 24 or 25 words controls your funds completely and permanently. Real support staff, wallet developers, exchanges and airdrop sites will never ask for it. Do not type it into any website, photograph it, save it in cloud notes or send it in a chat. Write it on paper and keep it somewhere safe, ideally in more than one place.
security.q7: How do I recognize common crypto scams?
security.a7: Be suspicious of: anyone who contacts you first offering help or giveaways; promises of guaranteed returns; urgent messages saying your wallet is "in danger"; websites that ask for your recovery phrase; unexpected tokens or NFTs that tell you to visit a website; and requests to sign something you do not understand. Verify links from an official source, bookmark the sites you use, and read every detail of a transaction before you sign - especially rekey requests, which hand control of your account to someone else.

accounts.title: Account Types & Setup
accounts.q1: What types of accounts can I create in {name}?
accounts.a1: {name} supports plain Ed25519 accounts (a standard private key), ARC-76 accounts derived deterministically from an email and password, HD (ARC-52 / BIP32-Ed25519) wallets that generate unlimited accounts from one recovery phrase, multisignature accounts requiring several approvals, Ledger hardware wallet accounts, post-quantum Falcon 1024 accounts, and rekeyed accounts that are controlled by a different key.
accounts.q2: What is an HD wallet and why would I use one?
accounts.a2: An HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallet stores a single 24-word recovery phrase and can derive an unlimited number of separate Algorand accounts from it, so you only ever need to back up one phrase instead of one per account. This is the recommended account type if you plan to manage many accounts.
accounts.q3: What is a multisignature (multisig) account and when should I use one?
accounts.a3: A multisignature account requires a minimum number of signatures from a chosen group of accounts before a transaction is valid, for example 2-of-3 co-signers. It is useful for shared treasuries, organizational funds, or any situation where you want to remove single points of failure from spending decisions.
accounts.q4: Can I use a Ledger hardware wallet with {name}?
accounts.a4: Yes. Ledger devices keep your private key isolated on the physical device and require you to physically confirm each transaction on its screen, which gives the highest level of protection against malware on your computer.
accounts.q5: How do I create a new account or import an existing one?
accounts.a5: From the accounts list, choose "New account" to generate a fresh Ed25519, HD, ARC-76, multisig, Ledger or post-quantum account, or choose "Import" to recover an account from an existing 25-word mnemonic, an HD recovery phrase, or a backup file exported from another device.
accounts.q6: Why is my brand new account not shown on the blockchain?
accounts.a6: Creating an account only generates a key pair on your device; the blockchain does not know about the address until someone sends it funds. An Algorand account must hold at least 0.1 ALGO (the minimum balance) to exist on-chain, so send at least that much to your new address - plus a little extra to cover fees - and it will appear.
accounts.q7: What is the difference between the 25-word and the 24-word recovery phrase?
accounts.a7: A standard Algorand account uses a 25-word mnemonic: 24 words encode the private key and the 25th is a checksum. An HD wallet uses a 24-word BIP-39 phrase from which many accounts are derived, so it can be used in other HD-compatible wallets too. The two are not interchangeable, so write down which type each phrase belongs to.

actions.title: Account Actions
actions.q1: How do I send and receive ALGO or assets?
actions.a1: Open an account and use the "Pay" action to send ALGO or any asset you have opted in to. To receive funds, share your account address or QR code from the "Receive" action. Before sending, check the address character by character and make sure the receiver is on the same network.
actions.q2: What does "opt-in" mean and why do I need to do it?
actions.a2: On Algorand an account must explicitly opt in to an asset before it can receive it. This protects you from being flooded with unwanted or scam tokens, and it means the ledger only stores balances that account owners actually asked for. Opting in is a zero-amount transfer to yourself: it costs the normal network fee (0.001 ALGO) and raises your account's minimum balance by 0.1 ALGO, which is not spent but locked while you hold the asset. You can opt in from the Assets tab of your account - or the wallet can offer it when you swap.
actions.q3: What is rekeying and what is it used for?
actions.a3: Rekeying changes which private key is allowed to sign for an account without changing the account's address, for example to move authority from a plain key to a multisig group or a Ledger device while keeping all assets, apps and history where they are. Only rekey to an address you fully control: whoever holds the new key controls the account, and only they can rekey it again. Scammers often disguise rekey requests as harmless transactions, so always read the rekey field before signing.
actions.q4: How do I schedule a future or recurring payment?
actions.a4: Use the Scheduled Payments feature on an account page to define a transaction template and a future date or recurring interval; {name}, via {link1} scheduler service, prepares the unsigned transaction and prompts you to sign and broadcast it when it becomes due.
actions.q5: How do I interact with a smart contract or DApp from {name}?
actions.a5: Connect {name} to the DApp using WalletConnect, either by scanning a QR code or pasting a connect URI, and every transaction the DApp requests appears in {name} for you to review in full detail and explicitly sign before anything is broadcast.
actions.q6: Why did my transaction fail or get rejected?
actions.a6: The most common reasons are: not enough ALGO to pay the amount, the fee and still keep the required minimum balance; sending an asset the receiver has not opted in to; sending an asset that you have not opted in to yourself; the transaction taking too long and expiring; or a smart-contract rule rejecting the call. {name} simulates payments on the node before signing, and the error message usually names the exact reason.
actions.q7: Do I need a memo or note when sending to an exchange?
actions.a7: Some exchanges use one shared address for many customers and require a memo (transaction note or tag) to know which customer to credit. Always read the deposit instructions of the exchange: if they ask for a memo, copy it exactly into the note field, otherwise your deposit may be delayed or lost. Also make sure you send the correct asset on the correct network, and test with a small amount first.
actions.q8: How do I opt out of an asset I no longer want?
actions.a8: On Algorand, opting out of an asset is done with a special transaction that closes the asset out of your account. This removes the asset and gives the 0.1 ALGO minimum-balance reserve back. Be careful: closing out sends any remaining balance of that asset to the address chosen in the transaction (usually the asset creator), so it cannot be recovered - send or swap the asset away first if it has any value.

assets.title: Assets & Tokens
assets.q1: What is an Algorand Standard Asset (ASA)?
assets.a1: An ASA is a token natively issued on the Algorand blockchain, using the same built-in mechanism for both fungible tokens (such as stablecoins or reward points) and non-fungible tokens (NFTs), without needing a separate smart contract per token as on some other chains. Every ASA has a unique Asset ID.
assets.q2: How do NFTs work on Algorand?
assets.a2: An Algorand NFT is simply an ASA with a total supply of 1 and 0 decimal places, usually with metadata (image, attributes) referenced through an IPFS or Arweave URL stored in the asset's configuration. {name} displays these media previews in your Assets tab.
assets.q3: Why do I see a small ALGO balance reserved that I can't spend?
assets.a3: Algorand requires every account to keep a minimum balance of 0.1 ALGO, plus 0.1 ALGO for each asset it has opted in to and additional amounts for the smart contracts it uses or stores data in. This prevents the ledger from being filled with empty or spam accounts. The reserve is released when you close out the asset or app that caused it.
assets.q4: How can I tell if a token is legitimate before opting in?
assets.a4: Anyone can create an ASA with any name or ticker, including fake tokens that impersonate well-known projects. Always verify the exact Asset ID on the issuing project's official website, and check the asset's creator address and details in {name} or a block explorer before opting in.
assets.q5: Can I hide unwanted or spam assets from my account view?
assets.a5: You can search and filter the table on the Assets tab by name, asset ID or amount to find what you need. Unsolicited tokens cannot be removed from the blockchain and cannot be used to take your funds, so you can safely ignore them - just never interact with the websites or messages that come with them.
assets.q6: Can an asset issuer freeze my tokens or take them back?
assets.a6: Possibly. When creating an ASA the issuer can set a freeze address, which can block an account from moving that asset, and a clawback address, which can move the asset out of any holder's account. Regulated assets such as some stablecoins use this on purpose; many other assets disable it permanently. The asset's details show which addresses are set - check them before you buy a token you plan to hold.
assets.q7: Someone sent me a token I never opted in to. Is that possible?
assets.a7: A normal ASA transfer cannot reach an account that has not opted in, so an unexpected asset means that your account opted in at some point - for example through a DApp request you signed - or that it is a different kind of token, such as an ARC-200 or an NFT you added. Some scams then tell you to visit a website to claim a prize. Ignore them: do not connect your wallet to it, and do not sign anything you did not initiate.

swap.title: Swapping & DeFi
swap.a1: The Swap page lets you exchange one Algorand asset for another directly from your wallet. {name} queries {link1} router to find the best price across multiple on-chain decentralized exchanges, then builds an unsigned transaction group that you review and sign yourself - funds never pass through a custodial intermediary.
swap.q2: What is slippage and why does the swap page ask me to set it?
swap.a2: Slippage tolerance is the maximum price movement you accept between the moment you request a quote and the moment your transaction settles on-chain. Set too low, your swap can fail in a fast-moving market; set too high, you may receive a worse price than expected.
swap.q3: What are liquidity pools and why do they determine my swap price?
swap.a3: A liquidity pool is a smart contract holding reserves of two assets that traders swap against. The price you get is set by the ratio of those reserves at the moment of your trade, and trades that are large relative to the pool move the price more (higher price impact).
swap.q4: Are there fees when I swap?
swap.a4: A swap involves the network fee for each transaction in the group, plus a small liquidity-provider fee charged by the DEX pool used. Both are shown in the swap preview before you confirm and sign.
swap.a5: No. Your assets stay under your own private key at every step. {name} only presents an unsigned transaction for the swap, which you must review and sign, exactly like any other transaction.
swap.q6: Why do I need to opt in to a token before I can swap into it?
swap.a6: Because Algorand only lets an account hold assets it has opted in to. If you have never held the token you want to receive, an opt-in is needed first, which costs the normal fee and locks 0.1 ALGO of minimum balance. Make sure you keep enough spare ALGO for this and for the swap fees.
swap.q7: How do I deposit USDC to earn interest and receive fUSDC?
swap.a7: Open the Swap page (Account > Swap) on Mainnet. If your account has not opted in to fUSDC yet, select USDC as the source asset and press "Opt in to fUSDC" - this reserves 0.1 ALGO of your minimum balance, and once the opt-in is confirmed fUSDC is selected as the destination asset automatically. To deposit, select USDC as the source asset and fUSDC as the destination asset and enter the amount (or press Max). The swap quote form is then replaced by the Folks Finance lending panel, which shows the fUSDC you receive, the current exchange rate and the APY - press Deposit and sign. To withdraw, press the ⇅ button (or select fUSDC as the source and USDC as the destination asset), enter the fUSDC amount and press Withdraw; you receive USDC at the current exchange rate (if you do not hold USDC yet, the opt-in is added automatically).
swap.q8: What is fUSDC and what are the risks?
swap.a8: fUSDC is the deposit token of the Folks Finance USDC lending pool. Your USDC is lent out to borrowers and the interest accrues in the exchange rate: one fUSDC becomes redeemable for more and more USDC over time, so your fUSDC balance itself does not grow. Deposits are not insured and carry smart-contract and protocol risk. A withdrawal can also fail temporarily if most of the pool is currently borrowed. The rate and APY are shown in the lending panel and change continuously. Folks lending is available on Mainnet only, and as with any transaction you must review and sign it yourself - funds are never held by {name}.

connect.title: WalletConnect & DApps
connect.q1: What is WalletConnect and why would I use it?
connect.a1: WalletConnect is an open protocol that lets {name} securely connect to third-party decentralized applications (DApps) - such as marketplaces, DEXs or games - running in another browser tab or device, so the DApp can request signatures without ever seeing your private key.
connect.q2: How do I connect {name} to a DApp?
connect.a2: Open the Connect page in {name}, enable the connection, then scan the QR code shown by the DApp with your camera or paste the "wc:" connection URI it provides. Approve the session request that appears and choose which of your accounts to expose to that DApp.
connect.q3: Is it safe to approve a transaction request from a DApp?
connect.a3: Only if you understand what it does. {name} decodes and displays every field of the requested transaction (type, sender, receiver, amount, asset, fee, rekey target and more) before you sign, so read the full detail instead of clicking Sign reflexively, especially for app calls and rekey requests.
connect.q4: How do I disconnect a DApp session?
connect.a4: Open the Connect page, find the active session under "Sessions", and select Disconnect. This immediately revokes the DApp's ability to send you further signing requests, though it can ask you to reconnect at any time.
connect.q5: What should I check to verify a DApp is genuine before connecting?
connect.a5: {name} highlights domain verification and network-mismatch warnings on incoming connection and transaction requests. Pay close attention to any "domain mismatch" or "unverified" warning, and only connect to DApp addresses you got from the project's official website or documentation.
connect.q6: Why does WalletConnect not start automatically when I open the wallet?
connect.a6: This is deliberate. The connection is only initialized after you choose to enable it, so nobody can send you signing requests that you do not expect while you are just checking your balance. Enable it when you want to use a DApp, and disconnect when you are finished.
connect.q7: What are Liquid Auth and ARC-14 authentication?
connect.a7: They are ways to prove that you own an account to a website or service, without sending any funds. Liquid Auth links your account to a passkey and connects to the DApp directly, peer to peer. ARC-14 asks you to sign a special login transaction that is never sent to the network. In both cases {name} clearly labels the request as an authentication, so you can see that it cannot move your money.

backup.title: Backup, Recovery & Support
backup.q1: How do I back up my wallet?
backup.a1: Open Settings, go to the Backup section, and export an encrypted backup file of your wallet to a location of your choice, such as a USB drive or password manager attachment. For individual accounts you can also record the 25-word mnemonic or HD recovery phrase, which works independently of {name}.
backup.q2: How can I move my wallet to another computer or browser?
backup.a2: Export a backup file from Settings on the original device, then on the new device choose "Import wallet" and upload that file. You unlock it with the same password as before, which you can change afterwards in Settings.
backup.q3: What happens if I forget my wallet password?
backup.a3: The password only unlocks the encrypted copy stored in that specific browser. It does not exist anywhere else, so without a backup the funds cannot be recovered - this is what makes the wallet secure. If you still have the recovery phrase of your accounts, you can re-import them and set a new password.
backup.q4: How can I view or contribute to the source code?
backup.a4: {name} is fully open source at {link1}; anyone may read, audit, fork or submit a pull request, and translation contributions are especially welcome via the src/locales folder.
backup.q5: How can I get help or support the project?
backup.a5: You can join the project's {link1} for community support, open an issue on {link2} for bugs or feature requests, contribute code or translations, or support ongoing development with a donation to the project's Algorand address listed in the app footer. {name} is not funded by Algorand Inc. or the Algorand Foundation, though it has received Algorand Foundation xGov community grants for specific features.
backup.q6: I cleared my browser data. Are my accounts gone?
backup.a6: Your wallet file lives in your browser's local storage, so clearing site data, uninstalling the browser or resetting the device deletes it. Your funds are still on the blockchain and can be recovered by importing the backup file or the recovery phrases of your accounts. This is why a backup made while you still have access is essential.

arc56.loading: Looking up this call in the ARC-56 contract registry…
arc56.trust_verified_desc: This app's actual on-chain program matches a registered ARC-56 specification, and it defines the exact method being called. The names and descriptions below come directly from that verified specification.
arc56.trust_verified_other_method_desc: This app's program is registered in the ARC-56 registry, but the method being called here is not part of its documented interface. This can mean the registry's copy is outdated, or that the app exposes an undocumented method — review the raw arguments carefully.
arc56.trust_selector_only: Unverified — method name recognized, but not this app
arc56.trust_selector_only_desc: This app's program itself is not registered. The method name and argument types shown below were matched only by the 4-byte method selector against other, unrelated apps in the registry — they are not verified against what this specific app actually does. Never assume the behavior matches.
arc56.trust_unknown: Unknown call — not found in the ARC-56 registry
arc56.trust_unknown_desc: Nothing about this call is recognized. Review the raw application arguments below carefully before signing.
arc56.trust_not_abi: Not a structured ABI method call
arc56.trust_not_abi_desc: This application call does not follow the ARC-4 ABI method-call format. See the raw application arguments below for the full, unmodified data.
arc56.candidates_desc: {count} other known app(s) expose a method with this same selector. You may optionally view one of them below to see suggested argument names — this is only a hint, never a verification of what this app actually does.
arc56.candidate_unverified_notice: These names and descriptions are unverified — they come from a different app's registered specification, not from the app you are actually calling.
arc56.required_txn_type: Requires a preceding "{type}" transaction in this group
arc56.no_arguments: This method call takes no arguments.
arc56.no_owners_found: No known GitHub publisher was found in the ARC-56 registry for this program - its source has not been indexed from any public repository, so you cannot verify who wrote it.
arc56.risk_trusted: Trusted: registry-verified contract from a low-risk publisher. This covers the smart-contract calls only - review the other transactions yourself.
arc56.risk_warning: Caution: this request could not be fully verified. Take extra care before signing.
arc56.risk_danger: High risk: do not sign unless you are certain what this does.
arc56.risk_not_abi: Not verifiable: none of the application calls in this request follow the ARC-4 ABI format, so the ARC-56 registry cannot describe them. Review the raw arguments carefully.
arc56.reason_banned_publisher: A publisher of this contract is on the registry ban list.
arc56.reason_method_mismatch: The called method is not part of the registered contract.
arc56.reason_unregistered: The contract program is not registered in the ARC-56 registry.
arc56.reason_low_reputation_publisher: The publisher's reputation is not rated low-risk.
arc56.reason_unrated_publisher: The publisher has no reputation rating.
arc56.reason_not_abi: Some application calls are not ABI calls and cannot be verified.
arc56.reason_sensitive_call: A call creates, updates, deletes, closes out of, or clears state of an application.
arc56.reason_risky_fields: Another transaction in this request closes out an account or asset holding, rekeys an account, claws back or freezes an asset, reconfigures an asset, or registers participation keys.
